description.value: This multi-visit, real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging feedback study examined whether treatment-seeking smokers could modulate behavioral and brain responses to smoking cues by decreasing activity in a craving-related region or increasing activity in a resistance-related region.

spans.text: This multi-visit, real-time functional magnetic resonance imaging feedback study demonstrates that treatment-seeking smokers can effectively modulate their behavioral and brain responses to smoking cues.

description.value: Participants attended three rtfMRI scanning visits, with an inter-visit interval of 7–10 days, and completed four runs at each visit; sixty percent completed all three visits.

spans.text: Eligible participants were scheduled to attend three rtfMRI scanning visits (inter-visit interval=7–10 days).
Fifteen right-handed, treatment-seeking, nicotine-dependent smokers (≥10 ciga-rettes/day, 21–45 years old) were recruited through local resources.
During each visit participants were exposed to four runs of an established nicotine cue-induced craving paradigm (blocks of smoking-related images, neutral-images, and rest) ( ).
During Neurofeedback runs (Runs 3 & 4) participants received simultaneous feedback via two thermometers following five smoking blocks, each independently driven by activity in the ROIs.
Compared to instructions to crave (Run 1; M =6.00), neurofeedback was most effective at reducing craving during Visit 3 (Run 3; M =4.78), t (8)=2.55, p =0.03.
